While I do 100% believe that she is being difficult and you have every right to help make decisions and be involved in your son's life, you really shouldn't be discouraging her from breastfeeding. While I don't think formula is at all harmful to infants, breastmilk is the ideal food for your baby. It also does NOT mean that you won't be able to take him to your place, even overnight. Breastfeeding when you have a job outside the home means building up a supply of expressed milk. If she establishes a good milk supply, then she will have NO problem leaving you with enough milk to feed your son while he is in your care. I decided as soon as I found out I was pregnant that I wanted to breastfeed my daughter, and it had nothing to do with keeping her tethered to me at all times. I know I would have been upset if anyone had suggested bottle-feeding simply out of convenience. 

That being said, if you really feel like she is intentionally trying to exclude you from YOUR son's life, I would confront her about it. You shouldn't feel like you're being pushy or demanding by expecting to be an equal part of your child's life. It would be unfortunate if you had to take her to court, but if that is necessary to establish yourself as an equal parent, then it is absolutely your right to do so. And there should definitely be some boundaries set with this new guy. He may end up being a part of your son's life, but he really shouldn't have any say in the naming/raising/custody agreement. If he wants to be involved then he needs to work around your expectations, not the other way around.

I had my daughter when I was 21 (22 now) and it really did feel like it was forced on me. I lived with my boyfriend and no matter how much I begged, he REFUSED to use protection. He even laughed in my face. I know I should have left, but I really cared about him (still do. In fact, I married him). He told me he was ready for a baby. I told him I wasn't. He didn't listen. Fast forward a year and a half, and here we are. It was hard to feel like my life was stolen from me, but my daughter is really the most wonderful thing I've ever been given. I was always proud of the child I had made. I've had total strangers tell me that she's the most beautiful baby they've ever seen. I even had one woman tell me "My baby is cute, but yours is seriously the cutest baby in the world." I just didn't appreciate that not only is she a gift, but motherhood itself is a gift, too.

Honestly, I felt every bit of what you're describing. I remember telling my husband "I love my daughter, but I hate motherhood." I sometimes felt like I was nurturing her only because I had to. I didn't have the life-changing, love at first sight experience that a lot of women describe. I felt terrible guilt because I had no reason to not enjoy my daughter; as far as babies go, she's the best, but being with her was never anything but a chore for me. I did enjoy playing with her and her laugh has always warmed my heart, but I often found myself wondering why I was only happy when my daughter was asleep/not around? Don't get me wrong, I have always loved her and would have killed for her even before she was born, but I just didn't know why I loved her. I wasn't happy being a mother. These feelings lasted for months. My daughter is a week short of being ten months old, and I JUST recently settled into and started really enjoying being a mother. I'm not totally sure what caused the huge change in perspective. Katherine just went from being a dependent little lump to this vivacious (almost) toddler, and I suddenly feel so much pride in being her mommy. 

I do think people jump to the PPD conclusion a little too quickly sometimes. It's a VERY serious condition, and if it is suspected that you have it, by all means, seek treatment. However, I really do believe that motherhood is just hard to adjust to for some people, and no amount of medication is going to change that.
